executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the erosion of institutional independence under political pressure, with the Justice Department's criminal inquiry into E. Jean Carroll standing as the most urgent and concrete manifestation of this trend. The decision to open a criminal investigation into a private citizen who successfully sued Donald Trump for sexual abuse and defamation raises direct and serious questions about whether federal prosecutorial power is being weaponized against perceived political adversaries — a development with profound implications for the rule of law. This connects directly to the Foreign Affairs newsletter's focus on NATO deterrence and Trump's foreign policy posture toward Iran, both of which hinge on the credibility and reliability of U.S. institutions as seen by allies and adversaries alike; when domestic rule-of-law norms appear compromised, America's leverage abroad is weakened proportionally. The Carroll inquiry is not an isolated news item but a signal about the current administration's willingness to deploy the machinery of government against critics and litigants, making it the story that most demands sustained attention today.

items.headline: Here's how the Spurs can force a Game 7
items.blurb: The San Antonio Spurs have their backs against the wall for the first time this postseason. They didn't face this — a loss away from their season being over — at any point in the first two rounds. Nobody has been surprised that the Spurs are good this season, but nobody expected 62 wins and a conference finals berth with a real shot at making the NBA Finals. However, the Thunder have reminded everybody that this era of basketball goes through OKC. Even with Victor Wembanyama letting them know his league ownership is nigh. The Spurs will have to figure out how to win two straight games against OKC, and that has to start tonight when the Spurs try to protect home court and keep their season alive in Game 6 (8:30 p.m. ET on NBC/Peacock).

newsletters.title: A summery shrimp and white bean dish

items.headline: Garlicky Shrimp With Summer Squash and Beans
items.blurb: If you add zucchini (or yellow squash) and briny clam juice to Sue Li's lemony shrimp and bean stew, a veritable New York Times Cooking classic, you get this beautiful new dish from Kay Chun. Kay's garlicky shrimp with summer squash and beans tastes almost as if Sue's dish took a coastal summer vacation — that clam juice gives the combination a saline lightness that makes it feel just right for warmer weather. Summer squash adds sweetness and heft; lemon juice, crushed red pepper and chives keep things bright. Like in Sue's dish, you'll want some bread on hand for swiping up all those garlicky juices, and leftovers are terrific tossed with pasta.

items.headline: Suya Spiced Grilled Chicken Thighs With Nectarines
items.blurb: OK, so I kind of already half-made this Yewande Komolafe recipe, in that I followed Step 1 to make that gingery, garlicky suya-spiced marinade for some bone-in, skin-on chicken pieces, then roasted them in the oven. Those results were so good that I'm extra compelled to complete Yewande's recipe as written, pairing those deeply savory chicken thighs with sweet-tart nectarines and fresh cilantro.

items.headline: Anchovy Carbonara
items.blurb: As someone who doesn't eat pork, I'm grateful to Cybelle Tondu for this recipe that captures all the lushness of the classic Roman pasta. This, with a tangle of arugula dressed with olive oil and lemon juice, is a perfect weeknight meal.

items.headline: Spicy Tomato and Pepper Curry
items.blurb: There's a stand at my favorite outdoor market that I simply call the pepper stand; they do sell other things (tomatoes, eggplants, the most perfect spherical onions you've ever seen) but oh, the peppers. So bright, so shiny, so ready for Zaynab Issa's vegan curry, which I may bulk up by adding eggs to simmer in the spiced tomato gravy, shakshuka-style.

newsletters.title: One thing that makes you feel successful

items.headline: Spencer Strider: Delayed gratification
items.blurb: Strider is a 27-year-old All-Star pitcher for the Atlanta Braves. His answer is in his words. Admiral William H. McRaven's 'Make Your Bed' speech: My high school coach, who was one of the most influential people in my life, showed us this when I was a freshman. And the first thing was: Make your bed. It's always stuck with me. Because I do think if you want to be organized, productive, thoughtful and present throughout the day, the first decision you make has to be that way, too. I'm a 'lay my clothes out for the next day' guy. When I start my day with that precise organization and focus, I've already taken away the stress of having to pick that outfit for the day. I'm saving myself time and energy. I fully believe in the paradox of choice. The fewer options, sometimes the better. Also, I am a crazy coffee guy. I would probably be a barista if I could, or if I had time. Every single place we go, I get coffee. I'm very deliberate about it. I scout out true 'third-wave' coffee shops. Seriously, I mean, I sit around all day and just think about that one cup of coffee I get to have the next day. It's my favorite part of the day. I try to force myself to do certain things, whatever that might be, before I give myself that cup of coffee. And that's because I'm a big delayed-gratification person. If I can make something harder for myself before I reward myself, then I've earned it. I really like that mentality. Then I can sit down. And I can really enjoy that coffee.

items.headline: Jessica Berman: Hugging her dogs
items.blurb: Berman is the 49-year-old commissioner of the National Women's Soccer League. Her answer is in her words. Dogs exude the most unconditional love anyone could imagine. It reminds me that those little doses of encouragement really can fuel everything you want to do in your life. It's a force multiplier. And so every moment I can, I lay down on the floor with my two dogs and let them pour all of their love and happiness and joy into me. My dogs are just such a simple reminder of the things that matter in life. They're very grounding for me. I got Charlie, who is the mutt, about five years ago during COVID, and I got Brooklyn, who is my golden, about two years ago. Abby, my third dog, passed away last year. She is actually the love of my life. We have a shrine for her, so I do feel that happiness and joy when I stand in front of her shrine, too. It gives me a lot of energy to continue to give when I'm not with them: In a world, and in a job, and in my life, that can all feel really chaotic — with a lot of people pulling on me and not knowing where I should be at any given minute — when I'm with them, I know that I'm exactly where I need to be. Because whatever I'm giving them is just … enough. And that is not a feeling I feel very often.

newsletters.title: Money Talks: How AI hides north-east Asia’s industrial rot

items.headline: Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are living a boom and a bust at once
items.blurb: Anyone glancing at the headlines in north-east Asia lately might think it is experiencing a golden age. Taiwan is currently expanding at a blistering 14%—growth rate virtually unheard of for a rich country. Operating profits at South Korea's biggest firms have ballooned by 159% over the past year. Both countries are seeing a tremendous export boom. Even sluggish Japan is seeing record corporate profits and exports. But beneath the staggering aggregate numbers lies surprising fragility. The region's export-led bonanza is almost entirely propped up by the artificial-intelligence boom. While world-bestriding manufacturers of semiconductors and servers for data centres race ahead, the rest of north-east Asia's industrial base is being quietly hollowed out.

newsletters.title: Climate tech companies are going public. What’s next?

items.headline: Climate tech companies are going public. What's next?
items.blurb:
Solar and battery company Solv Energy went public in February, hitting a $6 billion valuation. X-energy, which builds small modular nuclear reactors, followed at $11.5 billion. Then came geothermal company Fervo Energy, reaching a market cap of about $12.4 billion.

All three have been IPO success stories. And it doesn't feel like a coincidence that they're racing to provide electricity in an era of rising demand, driven partly by data centers.

What does this boom reveal about the future of the grid? And what comes next?

breaking_digest.narrative:
The Justice Department has opened a criminal inquiry into E. Jean Carroll, the writer who successfully sued Donald Trump for sexual abuse and defamation, according to people familiar with the matter [2]. The move marks a significant escalation and raises immediate questions about the independence of federal prosecutors, given Carroll's legal history with Trump. No charges have been announced, and details of the inquiry's scope remain limited [2].

Separately, CBS News made a significant leadership move at its flagship newsmagazine program, naming an outsider to lead '60 Minutes' [1]. The appointment signals a potential shift in direction for one of television's longest-running and most prestigious news programs, which has faced internal and external pressures in recent months [1].
